title: Galois objects dominate connected objects
statement: Let $(\mathcal C,F)$ be a Galois category [def-galois-category] and $X$ a connected object of $\mathcal C$ [def-galois-connected-object]. Then there are a Galois object $Z$ of $\mathcal C$ (a connected object such that $\operatorname{Aut}(Z)$ acts transitively on $F(Z)$, equivalently $\#\operatorname{Aut}(Z)=\#F(Z)$, as in [lem-galois-axioms](6)) and a morphism $Z\to X$. (The construction: the symmetric group acts on the $n$-fold product $X^n$, $n=\#F(X)$, and one takes a connected component of $X^n$ whose fibre contains a tuple of pairwise distinct elements.)

source.place: node lem-galois-object-exists, order 971; literature: literature/stacks-project/pione.tex, Fundamental Groups of Schemes, Lemma 0BN2 (label lemma-galois)

proof.text: Setup. By axiom (3) of [def-galois-category] $n=\#F(X)$ is finite, and $n\ge1$: $X$ is connected, hence not initial [def-galois-connected-object], so $F(X)\neq\emptyset$ by [lem-galois-axioms](3). The $n$-fold product $X^n$ with projections $\mathrm{pr}_1,\dots,\mathrm{pr}_n$ exists since $\mathcal C$ has finite limits [def-galois-finite-limits-colimits]. For $g\in S_n$ let $\sigma_g:X^n\to X^n$ be the morphism with $\mathrm{pr}_i\circ\sigma_g=\mathrm{pr}_{g^{-1}(i)}$; by the universal property of the product $\sigma_{gh}=\sigma_g\circ\sigma_h$ and $\sigma_1=\mathrm{id}$, so each $\sigma_g$ is an automorphism. Since $F$ is exact [def-galois-exact-functor] it preserves finite products, so $F(X^n)=F(X)^n$ via the $F(\mathrm{pr}_i)$, and $F(\sigma_g)$ is the permutation $(x_i)_i\mapsto(x_{g^{-1}(i)})_i$ of coordinates. By axiom (2) of [def-galois-category] write $X^n$ as a finite coproduct [def-galois-finite-coproduct] of connected objects, $\iota_t:Z_t\to X^n$ ($t\in T$, $T$ finite). $F$ preserves finite coproducts, so the maps $F(\iota_t)$ are injective and $F(X^n)$ is the disjoint union of their images; we identify $F(Z_t)$ with its image. Enumerate $F(X)=\{s_1,\dots,s_n\}$ (pairwise distinct) and let $t\in T$ be the unique index with $s=(s_1,\dots,s_n)\in F(Z_t)$.

source.place: Fundamental Groups of Schemes, Lemma 0BN2 (label lemma-galois), proof, first paragraph, first three sentences

proof.text: Claim 1: every $s'=(s'_1,\dots,s'_n)\in F(Z_t)$ has pairwise distinct coordinates. Suppose $s'_i=s'_j$ for some $i<j$ (so $n\ge2$). Let $\Delta_{ij}:X^{n-1}\to X^n$ be the morphism whose $k$-th component is the projection to the factor of $X^{n-1}$ indexed by $k$ for $k\neq j$ and equals the $i$-th of those for $k=j$ (index the factors of $X^{n-1}$ by $\{1,\dots,n\}\setminus\{j\}$). Under $F(X^{m})=F(X)^{m}$ the map $F(\Delta_{ij})$ is $u\mapsto$ the $n$-tuple with $j$-th coordinate $u_i$; its image is the set of tuples with equal $i$-th and $j$-th coordinate, so $s'=F(\Delta_{ij})(u)$ for some $u$. Write $X^{n-1}$ as a finite coproduct of connected objects $\kappa_w:W_w\to X^{n-1}$ (axiom (2)); $u$ lies in $F(W_w)$ for some $w$. By [lem-galois-axioms](7) applied to $\Delta_{ij}$ there are $t'\in T$ and $\delta:W_w\to Z_{t'}$ with $\Delta_{ij}\circ\kappa_w=\iota_{t'}\circ\delta$; since $F(\Delta_{ij})(u)=s'\in F(Z_t)$ and the $F(Z_{t''})$ are disjoint, $t'=t$. Now $\delta$ is a morphism between connected objects, hence an epimorphism by [lem-galois-axioms](4), hence $F(\delta)$ is surjective by [lem-galois-axioms](2). So $s=F(\iota_t)(s)=F(\Delta_{ij})(F(\kappa_w)(v))$ for some $v\in F(W_w)$, whence $s_i=s_j$, contradicting the distinctness of the $s_k$.

source.place: Fundamental Groups of Schemes, Lemma 0BN2 (label lemma-galois), proof, first paragraph: 'If $(s'_1,\ldots,s'_n)\in F(Z_t)$ is another element ... which is not the case' (the 'image of a connected component of $X^{n-1}$ under $\Delta_{ij}$' written out via Lemma 0BN0 (6), (3), (8))

proof.text: Claim 2: $\operatorname{Aut}(Z_t)$ acts transitively on $F(Z_t)$, so $Z_t$ is Galois. For $g\in S_n$, [lem-galois-axioms](7) applied to $\sigma_g\circ\iota_t:Z_t\to X^n$ (with $Z_t$ the coproduct of the single connected object $Z_t$) gives $t_g\in T$ and $\tau:Z_t\to Z_{t_g}$ with $\sigma_g\circ\iota_t=\iota_{t_g}\circ\tau$; by disjointness of the $F(Z_{t''})$, $t_g=t$ if and only if $F(\sigma_g)(s)\in F(Z_t)$. Let $G=\{g\in S_n: t_g=t\}$. For $g\in G$ the morphism $\tau_g:Z_t\to Z_t$ with $\iota_t\circ\tau_g=\sigma_g\circ\iota_t$ is unique because $\iota_t$ is a monomorphism ($F(\iota_t)$ is injective, [lem-galois-axioms](2)). If $g,h\in G$ then $\sigma_{gh}\circ\iota_t=\iota_t\circ\tau_g\circ\tau_h$, so $gh\in G$ and $\tau_{gh}=\tau_g\tau_h$, and $\tau_1=\mathrm{id}$; $G$ is a subgroup of the finite group $S_n$, so $g^{-1}\in G$ and each $\tau_g$ is an automorphism of $Z_t$ with inverse $\tau_{g^{-1}}$. Let $s'\in F(Z_t)$. By Claim 1 its coordinates are pairwise distinct, and as $n=\#F(X)$ the tuple $s'$ is another enumeration of $F(X)$; hence there is $g\in S_n$ with $F(\sigma_g)(s)=s'$. Then $F(\sigma_g)(s)\in F(Z_t)$, so $g\in G$, and $F(\tau_g)(s)=s'$ in $F(Z_t)$ (apply the injective $F(\iota_t)$). Thus $\operatorname{Aut}(Z_t)$ acts transitively on $F(Z_t)$; $Z_t$ is connected, so it is Galois by [lem-galois-axioms](6).

source.place: Fundamental Groups of Schemes, Lemma 0BN2 (label lemma-galois), proof, second paragraph ('Let $G\subset S_n$ be the subgroup of elements with $g(Z_t)=Z_t$ ... the action of $G$ on $F(Z_t)$ is transitive'), with the definition of Galois object in the paragraph after Lemma 0BN0

proof.text: Conclusion. $Z=Z_t$ is Galois by Claim 2, and $\mathrm{pr}_1\circ\iota_t:Z_t\to X$ is the required morphism.
